title: The convergence region of a series in the complex plane: where does it converge?
summary: A series with a complex variable converges in a disk (power series) or an annulus (Laurent series). Colouring the plane by convergence and drawing the boundary circles shows the region and its edges at a glance.

media.alt: Two panels of the complex plane. Left: a teal disk of radius 1 inside a rose region with a dashed orange boundary circle and a marked point at z = 1. Right: a teal annulus between circles of radius 1 and 3 with rose inside and outside, with dashed boundaries.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where does it converge?
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels: Re z horizontal and Im z vertical, from -4 to 4, equal scale. Teal: convergence. Rose: divergence. Dashed or dash-dot amber circles: boundaries (|z| = 1 in the left panel; |z| = 1 and |z| = 3 in the right). The cross at z = 1 marks the singularity on the boundary.
look_at: What is the shape of each convergence region and what sets its radius?
What lies on each boundary circle: convergence, divergence or a mix?
Why does the right panel have an inner disk that diverges?
Which point on the left boundary is special?
as_drawn: Left: sum z^n / n converges for |z| < 1 (radius R = 1), with a marked singularity at z = 1. Right: sum (z/3)^n + sum z^(-n), an annulus 1 < |z| < 3.
The boundaries are drawn as dashed lines with no statement of what happens on them. On the left circle, the series converges at every point except z = 1; the figure does not show this.
The inner disk of the right panel is labelled 'div.' in small type, and the colours encode only convergence or not, not the speed of convergence.
read_the_figure.proves: The open region where the series converges. Colour alone cannot tell absolute from conditional convergence, or give the behaviour on the boundary.
if_wrong: Boundary not marked: the reader assumes the region ends exactly at the circle.
Singularities not marked: the reason for the radius is invisible.
A hard colour edge: suggests a sharp change in value when the sum just converges more slowly near the boundary.

terms.meaning: A series in powers of z - a: sum of c_n (z - a)^n.
The distance within which a power series converges; set by the nearest singularity.
A series with negative and positive powers; converges on an annulus.
Convergence that depends on cancellation between terms, not on their absolute sizes.
If the limit of |a_(n+1)/a_n| is L, the series converges for L < 1 and diverges for L > 1.

remember: Power series converges in a disk; the radius is the distance to the nearest singularity.
Laurent series converges in an annulus.
The boundary needs a separate test: anything can happen there.
Mark the singularities and the boundary behaviour.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Colour fills encode converge or not (teal or rose); dashed amber circles are the boundaries; a cross marks a singularity; text names regions. Position is the complex plane; radius from the origin is |z|, which is why circles are the natural boundaries.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A series is a function of z only where it converges, and the region where it converges is determined by size, |z|, not by direction. That is why the regions are discs and rings: the picture shows that. The marked singularity on the boundary explains the radius: the function -ln(1 - z) is not defined at z = 1, and the radius stops there.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A dashed boundary line gives no information about what happens on the circle. The left series converges at z = -1 (to -ln 2) and diverges at z = 1, and the picture can't show that. Colour edges suggest abrupt change, but convergence just slows down near the boundary. And a region of convergence is not the domain of the underlying function: the function extends beyond.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: A marked boundary tells the reader exactly where the region stops, and a marked singularity says why. The convention is to label what happens on the boundary: without it a conditional convergence cannot be separated from divergence.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A real-line interval diagram is enough for real series. To see the rate of convergence colour by log of the n-th term at large n. To see the function beyond the disk, use domain colouring (F2.5) of the analytic continuation. A partial-sum error map shows where finite sums are accurate.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour the boundary circle point by point: teal where the series converges (all except z = 1), rose at z = 1, and mark z = -1 with its sum -ln 2.

steps.title: Radius by the ratio test
steps.note: The limit |z| < 1 gives R = 1; the sum is -ln(1 - z), which is singular at z = 1 and sets the radius. At z = 0.9 the partial sums reach 2.3026, the exact -ln 0.1.

steps.title: On the boundary and the annulus
steps.note: At z = -1 the partial sums reach -0.693145 after 2e5 terms (exact -0.693147); at z = 1 the harmonic sum is 12.78 after 2e5 terms and grows like ln n. At z = 2 the annulus sum is 2 + 1 = 3.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what is the radius on the left? (2) What are the radii on the right, and what does each bound? (3) What happens at the marked cross?

solution.text: 1: the teal disk ends at the dashed circle of radius 1.
Outer radius 3 bounds the geometric series in z/3; inner radius 1 bounds the series in 1/z, which needs |z| > 1.
z = 1 is the singularity of -ln(1 - z): the series is the harmonic series there and diverges, although it converges at every other point of the circle (for example at z = -1).

worked.answer: R = 1; annulus 1 < |z| < 3; at z = 1 the series diverges, at z = -1 it converges to -ln 2; the picture does not show the boundary behaviour.

analyze.q: Why are convergence regions of power series always discs?
analyze.hint: The ratio test depends on |z| only.

analyze.q: The series sum z^n / n has a singularity at z = 1. Why is there no singularity at z = -1, yet the radius is still 1?
analyze.hint: Radius is set by the nearest singularity at any angle.

analyze.q: What would the colour map show if we plotted the number of terms needed for 1e-6 accuracy?

checks.q: What is the shape of the region of convergence of a power series about 0?
checks.answer: A disk |z| < R (possibly with some boundary points).

checks.q: Apply the ratio test to z^n / n.
checks.answer: n/(n+1)|z| -> |z|, so converges for |z| < 1 and diverges for |z| > 1.

checks.q: A Laurent series converges for 1 < |z| < 3. What do the two radii each come from?
checks.answer: The series in positive powers sets the outer radius (3); the series in negative powers sets the inner radius (1).
